## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta* ("The Longer Discourse on the Ending of Craving", MN 38) is the thirty-eighth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The sutta is framed around the rebuke of the monk Sāti, who espoused the pernicious view that one and the same consciousness (*viññāṇa*) transmigrates through the round of rebirths to experience the results of good and bad deeds [Hung 2010; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Watanabe 1983]. To refute this misconception, the Buddha expounds dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), demonstrating that consciousness invariably arises dependent on conditions and does not exist as an enduring, independent entity [SuttaCentral; Hung 2010; Balasooriya et al. 1980].
Within this doctrinal refutation, the Buddha presents an analysis of the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*) [Watanabe 1983; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] and describes the twelve links of dependent origination in an immediate, timeless (*akālika*) manner [Balasooriya et al. 1980]. The discourse notes that one who attains direct insight into dependent arising abandons speculative questions regarding existence in the past or future [Anālayo 2018]. MN 38 also contains a well-known account of conception occurring through the convergence of three conditions: the coitus of the parents, the mother being in season (*utunī*), and the presence of the *gandhabba* (explained in the commentary MA ii 310 as the being driven by karma to enter the womb) [Balasooriya et al. 1980; Langenberg; Anālayo 2018]. Additionally, the text reiterates the raft simile (*kulla*) to caution monks against clinging dogmatically even to correct doctrinal views [IABU 2012], sharing substantial material with the *Alagaddūpama Sutta* (MN 22) [Anderson 1999; DharmaNexus].
Extensive textual parallels are preserved across traditions: curated parallels include Madhyama Āgama MĀ 201, Ekottarika Āgama EĀ 21.3, Saṃyukta Āgama SĀ 304, Tibetan *Upāyikā* Up 3.059, and Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta48 and sutta71) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus strongly aligns the text with MĀ 201 (T 26.54), the Tibetan *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094), the *Lalitavistara*, the *Nidānasaṃyukta*, and Vinaya texts such as the *Pravrajyāvastu* and *Saṅghabhedavastu* [DharmaNexus]. Internally, DharmaNexus records extensive text reuse with the *Nidāna Saṃyutta* (SN 12), the *Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta* (SN 35), the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga* (Vb 6), and gradual training pericopes shared with discourses such as MN 27, MN 51, MN 101, and AN 4.198 [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
